claim: FBXO45 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that is frequently elevated expression in human HCC.
source: FBXO45 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that is frequently elevated expression in human HCC.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about FBXO45.

claim: FBXO45 protein was highly expressed in 54.3% (57 of 105) of the HCC tissue samples.
source: IHC and qPCR analysis revealed that FBXO45 protein and mRNA were highly expressed in 54.3% (57 of 105) and 52.2% (132 of 253) of the HCC tissue samples, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC analysis data presented in the abstract and results section.

claim: FBXO45 mRNA was highly expressed in 52.2% (132 of 253) of the HCC tissue samples.
source: IHC and qPCR analysis revealed that FBXO45 protein and mRNA were highly expressed in 54.3% (57 of 105) and 52.2% (132 of 253) of the HCC tissue samples, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR analysis data presented in the abstract.

claim: Highly expressed FBXO45 promoted liver tumorigenesis in transgenic mice.
source: Highly expressed FBXO45 promoted liver tumorigenesis in transgenic mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FBXO45 transgenic mice presented in the abstract and results section.

claim: FBXO45 promoted IGF2BP1 ubiquitination at the Lys190 and Lys450 sites.
source: Mechanistically, FBXO45 promoted IGF2BP1 ubiquitination at the Lys190 and Lys450 sites and subsequent activation, leading to the upregulation of PLK1 expression and the induction of cell proliferation and liver tumorigenesis in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data presented in the abstract and results section.

claim: FBXO45-mediated IGF2BP1 ubiquitination leads to IGF2BP1 activation.
source: Mechanistically, FBXO45 promoted IGF2BP1 ubiquitination at the Lys190 and Lys450 sites and subsequent activation, leading to the upregulation of PLK1 expression and the induction of cell proliferation and liver tumorigenesis in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that ubiquitination at K190 and K450 increases IGF2BP1 activity.

claim: FBXO45-mediated IGF2BP1 activation leads to upregulation of PLK1 expression.
source: Mechanistically, FBXO45 promoted IGF2BP1 ubiquitination at the Lys190 and Lys450 sites and subsequent activation, leading to the upregulation of PLK1 expression and the induction of cell proliferation and liver tumorigenesis in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing PLK1 upregulation in response to FBXO45 overexpression.

claim: PLK1 inhibition significantly blocked FBXO45-driven liver tumorigenesis in FBXO45 transgenic mice.
source: PLK1 inhibition or IGF2BP1 knockdown significantly blocked FBXO45-driven liver tumorigenesis in FBXO45 transgenic mice, primary cells, and HCCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using PLK1 inhibitors in transgenic mice.

claim: IGF2BP1 knockdown significantly blocked FBXO45-driven liver tumorigenesis in FBXO45 transgenic mice.
source: PLK1 inhibition or IGF2BP1 knockdown significantly blocked FBXO45-driven liver tumorigenesis in FBXO45 transgenic mice, primary cells, and HCCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using IGF2BP1 knockdown in transgenic mice.

claim: There is a positive association between the hyperexpression of FBXO45 and PLK1 in HCC tissue samples.
source: Furthermore, IHC analysis on HCC tissue samples revealed a positive association between the hyperexpression of FBXO45 and PLK1/IGF2BP1, and both had positive relationship with poor survival in HCC patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC analysis data on HCC tissue samples.

claim: There is a positive association between the hyperexpression of FBXO45 and IGF2BP1 in HCC tissue samples.
source: Furthermore, IHC analysis on HCC tissue samples revealed a positive association between the hyperexpression of FBXO45 and PLK1/IGF2BP1, and both had positive relationship with poor survival in HCC patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC analysis data on HCC tissue samples.

claim: High FBXO45 expression has a positive relationship with poor survival in HCC patients.
source: Furthermore, IHC analysis on HCC tissue samples revealed a positive association between the hyperexpression of FBXO45 and PLK1/IGF2BP1, and both had positive relationship with poor survival in HCC patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data presented in the abstract and results section.

claim: HCC is a highly aggressive primary liver malignancy.
source: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a highly aggressive primary liver malignancy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Around 60% of HCC patients are diagnosed at advanced stages of carcinogenesis.
source: Currently, around 60% of HCC patients are diagnosed at advanced stages of carcinogenesis, consequently not able to receive potentially curative treatments (Altekruse et al., 2009; Cucchetti et al., 2013; Kanwal and Singal, 2019; Llovet et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HCC is a heterogeneous disease driven by the serial accumulation of mutations in tumor suppressor genes and proto-oncogenes.
source: Mounting evidence shows that HCC is a stepwise process, as HCC is a heterogeneous disease driven by the serial accumulation of mutations in tumor suppressor genes (such as TP53, PTEN, and RB) and proto-oncogenes (such as MYC, MET, BRAF, and RAS)(Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Ubiquitination is a posttranslational modification that can affect protein localization and regulate cell cycle progression, apoptosis, and transcriptional activity.
source: Ubiquitination is a posttranslational modification that can affect protein localization and regulate cell cycle progression, apoptosis, and transcriptional activity (Teixeira and Reed, 2013; DiAntonio et al., 2001; Meyer-Schwesinger, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ubiquitin-proteasome system involves enzymes in three distinct classes: E1, E2, and E3.
source: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is initiated by the conjugation of ubiquitin (a 76-amino acid polypeptide) to a substrate protein, which involves enzymes in three distinct classes of enzymes, a ubiquitin-activating enzyme (E1), ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2), and ubiquitin ligase (E3)(Micel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Micel et al., 2013.

claim: E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases are critical in the UPS for the selectivity needed to target specific proteins for degradation.
source: E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases are critical in the UPS for the selectivity needed to target specific proteins for degradation (Deshaies and Joazeiro, 2009; Nakayama and Nakayama, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HCC is associated with abnormal regulation of E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: Increased evidence has indicated that HCC is associated with abnormal regulation of E3 ubiquitin ligases (Shen et al., 2018; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: F-box protein is the substrate recognizing subunit of SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes.
source: F-box protein is the substrate recognizing subunit of SCF (SKP1, CUL1, and F-box protein) E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes (Chen et al., 2014) and plays important roles in cancer development and progression via regulation of the expression and activity of oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (Randle and Laman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FBXO45 is an atypical E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: F-box/SPRY domain-containing protein 1 (FBXO45) is an atypical E3 ubiquitin ligase (Saiga et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Saiga et al., 2009.

claim: FBXO45 promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis of FBXW7.
source: FBXO45 promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis of some key molecules governing cell survival or DNA damage, in which include FBXW7 (Richter et al., 2020), PAR4 (prostate apoptosis response protein 4) (Chen et al., 2014), p73 (Peschiaroli et al., 2009), and ZEB1 (Wu et al., 2019) and it can also block the proteolysis of some proteins, including N-cadherin (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 2020.

claim: FBXO45 promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis of PAR4.
source: FBXO45 promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis of some key molecules governing cell survival or DNA damage, in which include FBXW7 (Richter et al., 2020), PAR4 (prostate apoptosis response protein 4) (Chen et al., 2014), p73 (Peschiaroli et al., 2009), and ZEB1 (Wu et al., 2019) and it can also block the proteolysis of some proteins, including N-cadherin (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: FBXO45 promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis of p73.
source: FBXO45 promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis of some key molecules governing cell survival or DNA damage, in which include FBXW7 (Richter et al., 2020), PAR4 (prostate apoptosis response protein 4) (Chen et al., 2014), p73 (Peschiaroli et al., 2009), and ZEB1 (Wu et al., 2019) and it can also block the proteolysis of some proteins, including N-cadherin (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peschiaroli et al., 2009.

claim: FBXO45 promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis of ZEB1.
source: FBXO45 promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis of some key molecules governing cell survival or DNA damage, in which include FBXW7 (Richter et al., 2020), PAR4 (prostate apoptosis response protein 4) (Chen et al., 2014), p73 (Peschiaroli et al., 2009), and ZEB1 (Wu et al., 2019) and it can also block the proteolysis of some proteins, including N-cadherin (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2019.

claim: FBXO45 can block the proteolysis of N-cadherin.
source: FBXO45 promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis of some key molecules governing cell survival or DNA damage, in which include FBXW7 (Richter et al., 2020), PAR4 (prostate apoptosis response protein 4) (Chen et al., 2014), p73 (Peschiaroli et al., 2009), and ZEB1 (Wu et al., 2019) and it can also block the proteolysis of some proteins, including N-cadherin (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: Nearly 54.2% of HCC patients had high FBXO45 expression in HCC tissues compared with adjacent normal tissues.
source: Recently, IHC staining showed that nearly 54.2% of HCC patients had high FBXO45 expression in HCC tissues compared with adjacent normal tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC staining data presented in the introduction.

claim: IGF2BP1 is an oncogenic protein expressed in various cancers, including HCC.
source: Insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 1 (IGF2BP1) is an oncogenic protein expressed in various cancers, including HCC.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: IGF2BP1 affects the proliferation and tumorigenic potential of leukemia cells through HOXB4, MYB, and ALDH1A1.
source: For example, IGF2BP1 affects the proliferation and tumorigenic potential of leukemia cells through the critical regulators of self-renewal HOXB4 and MYB and the aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH1A1 (Elcheva et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Elcheva et al., 2019.

claim: IGF2BP1 increases melanoma metastasis via extracellular vesicle-mediated promotion.
source: IGF2BP1 increases melanoma metastasis via extracellular vesicle-mediated promotion (Ghoshal et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ghoshal et al., 2019.

claim: IGF2BP1 enhances the expression of various serum response factor (SRF) target genes, including PDLIM7, FOXK1, MKI67, and MYC.
source: IGF2BP1 enhances the expression of various serum response factor (SRF) target genes, including PDLIM7, FOXK1, MKI67, and MYC, and promotes tumor cell growth and invasion in HCC and other cancers (Gutschner et al., 2014; Müller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gutschner et al., 2014 and Müller et al., 2018.

claim: IGF2BP1 has suppressive roles in tumor growth and metastasis in breast cancer and colon cancer.
source: However, a few recent studies found that suppressive roles for IGF2BP1 in tumor growth and metastasis in breast cancer and colon cancer (Wang et al., 2016; Hamilton et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2016 and Hamilton et al., 2015.

claim: Hyperexpression of FBXO45 was correlated with poor prognosis in HCC.
source: Here, hyperexpression of FBXO45 was correlated with poor prognosis in HCC.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data presented in the results section.

claim: FBXO45 significantly promoted HCC tumorigenesis in FBXO45-OE mice.
source: Furthermore, FBXO45 significantly promoted HCC tumorigenesis in FBXO45-OE (OE as over-expressed) mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FBXO45-OE mice.

claim: FBXO45 specifically bound to IGF2BP1.
source: Mechanistically, FBXO45 specifically bound to IGF2BP1 and promoted its ubiquitination and activation, followed by upregulation of PLK1.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data presented in the results section.

claim: IGF2BP1 was identified as a novel substrate of FBXO45.
source: IGF2BP1 was identified as a novel substrate of FBXO45.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry and ubiquitination assay data.

claim: Targeting IGF2BP1-PLK1 signaling significantly attenuated HCC tumorigenesis triggered by FBXO45.
source: Targeting IGF2BP1-PLK1 signaling significantly attenuated HCC tumorigenesis triggered by FBXO45.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using IGF2BP1 knockdown and PLK1 inhibitors.

claim: FBXO45 expression was significantly increased in 54.3% (57/105) of the HCC samples compared with the adjacent noncancerous tissue samples.
source: IHC staining results showed that FBXO45 expression was significantly increased in 54.3% (57/105) of the HCC samples compared with the adjacent noncancerous tissue samples (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: High expression of FBXO45 localized to HCC cells but not hepatic stellate cells or fibrotic cells.
source: This high expression of FBXO45 localized to HCC cells but not hepatic stellate cells (HSCs; identified by alpha-smooth muscle actin [α-SMA], a well-established marker of HSCs in the fibrotic liver) or fibrotic cells (Sirius red signal, an indicator of fibrotic cells), implying that the expression of FBXO45 was restricted to HCC cells (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: FBXO45 was overexpressed in HCC tissue compared with normal tissue in two data sets.
source: Strikingly, gene expression analysis of two data sets revealed that FBXO45 was overexpressed in HCC tissue compared with normal tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Chen et al., 2002; Wurmbach et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis data from two published datasets.

claim: FBXO45 expression was positively associated with tumor size in HCC samples.
source: IHC analysis on HCC samples showed that FBXO45 expression was positively associated with tumor size, tumor differentiation, and TNM stage (Figure 1C–E and Table 1), indicating that FBXO45 expression positively correlated with HCC disease progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC analysis data shown in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: FBXO45 expression was positively associated with tumor differentiation in HCC samples.
source: IHC analysis on HCC samples showed that FBXO45 expression was positively associated with tumor size, tumor differentiation, and TNM stage (Figure 1C–E and Table 1), indicating that FBXO45 expression positively correlated with HCC disease progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC analysis data shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: FBXO45 expression was positively associated with TNM stage in HCC samples.
source: IHC analysis on HCC samples showed that FBXO45 expression was positively associated with tumor size, tumor differentiation, and TNM stage (Figure 1C–E and Table 1), indicating that FBXO45 expression positively correlated with HCC disease progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC analysis data shown in Figure 1E and Table 1.

claim: FBXO45 is an independent risk factor for poor OS in HCC patients (OS, hazard ratio [HR]: 2.447; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.490–4.021; p<0.001).
source: Univariate and multivariate analyses demonstrated that FBXO45 (p<0.001), tumor differentiation (p=0.021), and metastasis status (p=0.002) were significantly associated with OS in HCC patients, suggesting that FBXO45 is an independent risk factor for poor OS in HCC patients (OS, hazard ratio [HR]: 2.447; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.490–4.021; p<0.001, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate analysis data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: FBXO45 expression in HCC patients was positively correlated with poor survival (p<0.0001).
source: Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated that FBXO45 expression in HCC patients was positively correlated with poor survival (p<0.0001; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The expression of FBXO45 was significantly correlated with AFP in TCGA database.
source: Strikingly, data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database showed that the expression of FBXO45 was significantly correlated with AFP, tumor differentiation, tumor stage, and TNM stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA database analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: The expression of FBXO45 was significantly correlated with tumor differentiation in TCGA database.
source: Strikingly, data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database showed that the expression of FBXO45 was significantly correlated with AFP, tumor differentiation, tumor stage, and TNM stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA database analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: The expression of FBXO45 was significantly correlated with tumor stage in TCGA database.
source: Strikingly, data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database showed that the expression of FBXO45 was significantly correlated with AFP, tumor differentiation, tumor stage, and TNM stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA database analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: The expression of FBXO45 was significantly correlated with TNM stage in TCGA database.
source: Strikingly, data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database showed that the expression of FBXO45 was significantly correlated with AFP, tumor differentiation, tumor stage, and TNM stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA database analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: FBXO45 was an independent prognostic marker in HCC (p=0.041) according to TCGA database.
source: Furthermore, FBXO45 was an independent prognostic marker in HCC (p=0.041; Supplementary file 3), and high FBXO45 expression was positively related to poor survival in HCC patients (p=0.03; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA database analysis shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: High FBXO45 expression was positively related to poor survival in HCC patients (p=0.03) according to TCGA database.
source: Furthermore, FBXO45 was an independent prognostic marker in HCC (p=0.041; Supplementary file 3), and high FBXO45 expression was positively related to poor survival in HCC patients (p=0.03; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA database analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The high FBXO45 expression in FBXO45-OE mice resulted in more tumors in the liver than the low FBXO45 expression in WT mice at up to 24 weeks post-injection.
source: The high FBXO45 expression in FBXO45-OE mice (n=11) resulted in more tumors in the liver than the low FBXO45 expression in WT mice (n=20) at up to 24 weeks post-injection, indicating that high FBXO45 expression drives hepatocarcinogenesis in mice (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FBXO45-OE mice shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: FBXO45-OE mice developed a high liver:body weight ratio compared with WT mice.
source: Furthermore, compared with WT mice, FBXO45-OE mice developed a high liver:body weight ratio (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The cell proliferation markers Mki67, Pcna, Ccnb1, and Ccnb2 were significantly upregulated in the FBXO45-OE mice compared with the WT mice.
source: In line with this finding, the cell proliferation markers Mki67, proliferating cell nuclear antigen (Pcna), cyclin B1 (Ccnb1), and cyclin B2 (Ccnb2) were significantly upregulated in the FBXO45-OE mice compared with the WT mice (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and IHC data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The transcription of fibrotic genes (Acta2, Timp1, Col1a1, Col1a2, Pdgfb, and Pdgfrb) was significantly increased in the FBXO45-OE mice.
source: The results showed that the transcription of the predominant fibrotic genes, including Acta2, tumor inhibitor of metalloproteinase 1 (Timp1), collagen type 1 alpha 1 (Col1a1), collagen type 1 alpha 2 (Col1a2), platelet-derived growth factor β (Pdgfb), and platelet-derived growth factor receptor β (Pdgfrb), was significantly increased in the FBXO45-OE mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The expression of inflammatory markers (Il6, Il1b, Tnfa, and Ccl2) was dramatically increased in the FBXO45-OE mice.
source: Furthermore, the expression of inflammatory markers, including interleukin Il6, Il1b, tumor necrosis factor α (Tnfa), and monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (Ccl2), was dramatically increased in the FBXO45-OE mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Hepatic fibrosis and inflammation were involved in the development of HCC triggered by FBXO45.
source: Thus, hepatic fibrosis and inflammation were involved in the development of HCC triggered by FBXO45.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing increased fibrotic and inflammatory markers in FBXO45-OE mice.

claim: Primary FBXO45-OE hepatocytes grew significantly faster compared with WT cells.
source: Compared with WT cells, primary FBXO45-OE hepatocytes grew significantly faster (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The expression of the proliferation markers Mki67, Pcna, and Ccnb1 was upregulated in FBXO45-OE cells.
source: In line with this finding, the expression of the proliferation markers Mki67, Pcna, and Ccnb1 was upregulated in FBXO45-OE cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Overexpression of FBXO45 promoted cell proliferation and colony formation in human HCC cells.
source: Also, overexpression of FBXO45 promoted cell proliferation and colony formation in human HCC cells (Figure 2I–K), while silencing of FBXO45 inhibited these capacities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation and colony formation assay data shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: Silencing of FBXO45 inhibited cell proliferation and colony formation in human HCC cells.
source: Also, overexpression of FBXO45 promoted cell proliferation and colony formation in human HCC cells (Figure 2I–K), while silencing of FBXO45 inhibited these capacities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation and colony formation assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: Six interacting proteins had more than 1.5-fold changes in ubiquitinated protein level in the Flag-FBXO45 group compared with the control group.
source: Six interacting proteins had more than 1.5-fold changes in ubiquitinated protein level in the Flag-FBXO45 group compared with the control group (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4.

claim: IGF2BP1 was one of the most upregulated oncogenes and played a critical role in the induction of HCC tumorigenesis in previous studies.
source: IGF2BP1 was one of the most upregulated oncogenes and played a critical role in the induction of HCC tumorigenesis in previous studies (Gutschner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gutschner et al., 2014.

claim: FBXO45 bound to endogenous IGF2BP1 in HCCLM3 and HepG2 cells.
source: FBXO45, upon ectopic expression in HCCLM3 or HepG2 cells, pulled down endogenous IGF2BP1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Endogenous IGF2BP1 pulled down ectopically expressed FBXO45.
source: Reciprocally, endogenous IGF2BP1 pulled down ectopically expressed FBXO45 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: WT FBXO45, but not its F-box domain-deleted mutant (FBXO45ΔF), pulled down IGF2BP1 in both HepG2 and HCCLM3 cells.
source: Significantly, WT FBXO45, but not its F-box domain-deleted mutant(FBXO45ΔF), pulled down IGF2BP1 in both HepG2 and HCCLM3 cells (Figure 3D), while both WT FBXO45 and FBXO45ΔF pulled down N-cadherin (a FBXO45 target protein binding the Sprouty domain) (Chung et al., 2014; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that IGF2BP1 interacted with FBXO45 at the F-box domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: IGF2BP1 interacted with FBXO45 at the F-box domain.
source: Significantly, WT FBXO45, but not its F-box domain-deleted mutant(FBXO45ΔF), pulled down IGF2BP1 in both HepG2 and HCCLM3 cells (Figure 3D), while both WT FBXO45 and FBXO45ΔF pulled down N-cadherin (a FBXO45 target protein binding the Sprouty domain) (Chung et al., 2014; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that IGF2BP1 interacted with FBXO45 at the F-box domain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that only WT FBXO45, not the F-box deleted mutant, binds IGF2BP1.

claim: FBXO45 and IGF2BP1 were co-localized in cytoplasm.
source: In addition, FBXO45 and IGF2BP1 were co-localized in cytoplasm, which further supports the binding of these two proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IGF2BP1 in HCC exhibited the upregulated ubiquitination at Lys190 and Lys450.
source: Based on the analysis of the ubiquitome shown in Figure 3A, we found that IGF2BP1 in HCC exhibited the upregulated ubiquitination at Lys190 and Lys450.
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitome analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The K190 and K450 sites of IGF2BP1 are evolutionarily conserved among different species.
source: Here, these two sites were evolutionarily conserved among different species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FBXO45 enhanced IGF2BP1 polyubiquitination.
source: As shown in Figure 3E, FBXO45 enhanced IGF2BP1 polyubiquitination, while the K190A or K450A mutants significantly blocked this action.
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The K190A or K450A mutants significantly blocked FBXO45-mediated IGF2BP1 polyubiquitination.
source: As shown in Figure 3E, FBXO45 enhanced IGF2BP1 polyubiquitination, while the K190A or K450A mutants significantly blocked this action.
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A K63R ubiquitin mutant significantly attenuated the formation of polyubiquitin chain to IGF2BP1 compared with both WT and a K48R mutant form of ubiquitin.
source: The in vivo ubiquitination assay indicated that a K63R ubiquitin mutant significantly attenuated the formation of polyubiquitin chain to IGF2BP1 compared with both WT and a K48R mutant form of ubiquitin (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: FBXO45 promoted K63-linked polyubiquitination of IGF2BP1.
source: In line with this finding, K48 ubiquitin attenuated IGF2BP1 polyubiquitination compared with K63 and WT ubiquitin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which further confirmed that FBXO45 promoted K63-linked polyubiquitination of IGF2BP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Knockdown of PAM could significantly block FBXO45-mediated IGF2BP1 ubiquitination.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, knockdown of PAM could significantly block FBXO45-mediated IGF2BP1 ubiquitination.
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: IGF2BP1 interacted with SKP1 but not cullin-1.
source: Furthermore, IGF2BP1 interacted with SKP1 but not cullin-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: FBXO45-PAM-SKP1 promoted K63-linked ubiquitination of IGF2BP1.
source: Taken together, FBXO45-PAM-SKP1 promoted K63-linked ubiquitination of IGF2BP1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that FBXO45 promotes K63-linked ubiquitination of IGF2BP1 and requires PAM and SKP1.

claim: MG132 did not significantly increase IGF2BP1 protein level compared with FBXO45-overexpressed alone group.
source: In addition, MG132, an inhibitor of proteasome, did not significantly increase IGF2BP1 protein level compared with FBXO45-overexpressed alone group, indicating that FBXO45 doesn't mediate IGF2BP1 proteasome-dependent degradation in HCCs (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: FBXO45 doesn't mediate IGF2BP1 proteasome-dependent degradation in HCCs.
source: In addition, MG132, an inhibitor of proteasome, did not significantly increase IGF2BP1 protein level compared with FBXO45-overexpressed alone group, indicating that FBXO45 doesn't mediate IGF2BP1 proteasome-dependent degradation in HCCs (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that MG132 treatment does not increase IGF2BP1 levels.

claim: WT IGF2BP1 dramatically promoted HCC proliferation, whereas K190A and K450A mutants attenuated its oncogenic activity.
source: WT IGF2BP1 dramatically promoted HCC proliferation, whereas K190A and K450A mutants attenuated its oncogenic activity (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: FBXO45 promoted WT IGF2BP1-mediated cell proliferation much stronger than two IGF2BP1 mutants (K190A and K450A).
source: In line with this finding, FBXO45 promoted WT IGF2BP1-mediated cell proliferation much stronger than two IGF2BP1 mutants (K190A and K450A) (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The ubiquitination of IGF2BP1 at K190 and K450 was positively related to its oncogenic activity, which was mediated by FBXO45.
source: Taken together, the ubiquitination of IGF2BP1 at K190 and K450 was positively related to its oncogenic activity, which was mediated by FBXO45.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that K190A and K450A mutants have reduced oncogenic activity.
